body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Logistics
What separates informed decisions about Logistics from costly guesswork in business? Primary context, measurable criteria, and disciplined execution form the foundation of lasting value.

Most operators overlook how Logistics drives unit economics and competitive moats at scale. Understanding its real-world mechanics reveals why disciplined organizations outperform during market shifts.

Logistics is the part of supply chain management that deals with the efficient forward and reverse flow of goods, services, and related information from the point of origin to the point of consumption according to the needs of customers.

The word logistics comes from the French logistique, which the Swiss military writer Antoine-Henri Jomini either coined or popularised and which appears in English from 1846, he linked it to logis ("lodgings"), though some sources instead trace it to the Greek logistikós. A logistician is a professional working in the field of logistics management.

Logistics management is a component that holds the supply chain together. The resources managed in logistics include physical goods such as materials, equipment, and foodstuffs, and also intangible items such as time and information.

Military logistics is concerned with maintaining army supply lines with food, armaments, ammunition, and spare parts, apart from the transportation of troops themselves. Civil logistics deals with acquiring, moving, and storing raw materials, semi-finished goods, and finished goods.
